options: A cold start: the model or server instance had to load or spin up
explanation: Serverless or scaled-to-zero deployments may need to load weights or start containers on the first request. Mitigations include keep-warm instances, minimum replicas and warm-up requests.

text: In a Compose or React style UI, what does 'unidirectional data flow' mean?
options: State flows down to the UI and events flow up to update a single source of truth
Data only moves sideways between screens
The UI edits the database directly
Every widget keeps its own copy of the data
explanation: A single source of truth with state going down and events going up makes UI behaviour predictable and testable. In Android this is commonly implemented with a ViewModel exposing StateFlow.

text: Which caching pattern writes to both the cache and the database as part of the same write operation to keep reads fresh, at the cost of slower writes?
explanation: Write-through updates the cache synchronously with the store, so subsequent reads see fresh data but each write pays extra latency. Cache-aside loads on demand and invalidates or updates on change.

text: A rate limiter runs INCR and then, in a separate command, EXPIRE. Why is this risky?
options: INCR cannot be used on numbers
If the process fails between the commands the key may never expire; use an atomic script or a command that sets both
explanation: Two separate steps are not atomic. A crash or error in between leaves a counter without TTL, blocking users forever. Use atomic operations such as SET with EX, a Lua script or a transaction.

text: You add read replicas to scale database reads. Which new issue can appear?
options: Replication lag: a user may not immediately see data they just wrote
explanation: Replicas apply changes asynchronously, so reads may be slightly behind. Route read-your-own-writes cases to the primary or use session-level consistency strategies.

text: A read-heavy feed page joins six tables and is slow. Which option can help, and what is its cost?
options: A precomputed denormalised table or materialised view; it costs extra storage and possible staleness
explanation: Precomputing the joined result trades storage and freshness for fast reads. Refresh it on a schedule or on change, and check the query plan and indexes before denormalising.

text: Turing's 1936 result on the halting problem has a practical consequence for tools that analyse code. Which one?
options: No analyser can perfectly decide every behaviour of every program, so tools accept false positives or negatives
Compilers must be slower than interpreters
explanation: There is no general algorithm that decides whether any program halts, and by extension many non-trivial properties are undecidable in general. Practical linters and verifiers trade completeness, soundness and speed.

text: Even with a huge hash space, hash tables still need collision handling. Which idea explains why collisions appear sooner than intuition suggests?
options: The pigeonhole principle only applies to small tables
The birthday paradox: collisions become likely after roughly the square root of the space size
explanation: With N possible hash values, collisions become likely after about √N items, not N. That is why robust tables chain or probe on collisions and why cryptographic hashes need long outputs.

text: In JavaScript, why does `setTimeout(fn, 0)` run fn after the current synchronous code finishes?
options: JavaScript pauses all code for a second
The callback is placed in a task queue and runs only when the call stack is empty
Timers run on a separate thread that edits variables
explanation: JavaScript runs one call stack; timers hand their callbacks to the event loop, which executes them after the current code completes. Even a 0 ms delay does not interrupt running code.

text: How are 'scaling laws' in LLM research best described?
options: Laws of physics proven by mathematics
Guarantees that bigger models are always better
Empirical regularities showing how loss tends to improve predictably with compute, data and parameters
explanation: Despite the word 'law', these are fitted trends from experiments. They guide planning but can change with architecture, data quality and evaluation, and do not guarantee gains on every task.

text: After a redesign, a site's overall conversion rate rose, yet it fell in both the mobile and desktop segments. Which explanation fits?
options: Simpson's paradox: the traffic mix shifted toward a higher-converting segment
explanation: Aggregates can reverse when groups of different sizes and rates change proportion. Always inspect segments and confounders before concluding that a change worked or failed.

text: What is a 'glitch token'?
options: A token that is always one character
A token used for punctuation only
A vocabulary entry that was rarely or never seen in training, so its embedding is poorly learned and can cause odd behaviour
explanation: If a string earned a vocabulary slot (for example from the tokenizer's data) but barely appears in model training, the model may handle it unpredictably. It is an artefact of separate tokenizer and model training.

text: A chatbot has a 500-token system prompt. Each turn adds a 150-token user message and a 250-token reply, and the full history is resent each time. Across 8 turns, how many input tokens are billed in total?
explanation: Request k sends 500 + 150 + 400×(k−1) tokens. Summing for k = 1..8: 8×650 + 400×28 = 5,200 + 11,200 = 16,400. Ignoring the resent history (5,200) badly underestimates cost; trim or summarise history.

text: Why do language models often fail at tasks like counting the letter 'r' in a word?
options: They see sub-word tokens rather than individual letters
explanation: A word may be one or two tokens, so letter-level structure is not directly visible to the model. Spelling out the word letter by letter, or using code, helps.

text: For Arabic retrieval systems, why do engineers often normalise text (for example alef variants, diacritics, tatweel) before indexing?
options: So spelling variants of the same word match, while the original text is kept for display
To change the meaning of words
To reduce the file size only
explanation: Arabic has orthographic variants that users type inconsistently. Normalising for search and matching improves recall, but aggressive normalisation can merge distinct words, so test it and keep the original for display.

text: You use an LLM as a judge to compare two prompt versions. Which known bias should you control for?
options: Position and verbosity bias: judges may favour the first answer or longer answers
explanation: LLM judges can be swayed by order and length. Randomise or swap positions, use clear rubrics, and spot-check with human review, especially for decisions that matter.

text: You let an AI agent run shell commands in your project. Which setup is safest?
options: Run it as an administrator on your main machine with no review
Use a sandbox or container with least privilege, no production secrets and review of risky commands
explanation: Agents can execute harmful commands through error or injected instructions. Isolation, minimal permissions, approvals for destructive actions and version control limit the damage.

text: What reduces factual hallucinations more reliably than only lowering the temperature?
options: Grounding the answer in retrieved sources, requiring citations and allowing the model to say it does not know
explanation: Low temperature reduces randomness but does not give the model facts. Retrieval plus a permitted 'unknown' answer and source checks address the actual cause: lack of grounded information.

text: You need a consistent set of crisp, scalable UI icons. Which approach is generally best?
options: Use a vector icon set or design tool, optionally with AI for ideas
Generate each icon with a raster image generator and trust the style to match
Draw them in a text editor
explanation: UI icons need exact geometry, consistent stroke and clean scaling, which vector tools provide. Raster generators vary between outputs and give pixel images that blur when scaled.

text: You process scanned Arabic documents with OCR. Which practice most improves reliability?
options: Assume OCR is perfect for Arabic
Choose an engine with Arabic support, test it on representative scans and verify mixed text, numbers and reading order
explanation: Arabic OCR must handle connected letters, diacritics, right-to-left order and embedded Latin text or numerals. Measuring error rates on your own scans shows whether post-processing or manual review is needed.

text: A research agent returns a 20-page report with 60 citations. What is an efficient quality check?
options: Open a sample of the citations, focusing on the claims that matter most, and check that the pages really support them
Trust it because it is long
Ask the agent if it is sure
explanation: Length and citation count do not prove accuracy. Verifying high-impact claims and a random sample estimates reliability; asking the same system to confirm itself is weak evidence.

text: A hypothetical model charges $3 per 1M input tokens. An app sends 120,000-token prompts 10,000 times a day, while a retrieval design would send 6,000 tokens. What is the approximate daily input saving?
explanation: Long prompts: 120,000 × 10,000 = 1.2B tokens → $3,600. Retrieval: 6,000 × 10,000 = 60M tokens → $180. Saving ≈ $3,420 per day, before comparing quality and any retrieval infrastructure cost. Prices here are illustrative.

text: A model scores perfectly on a single-fact 'needle in a haystack' test, yet fails on your task that requires combining many facts across a long document. Why?
options: Finding one planted fact is easier than aggregating or reasoning over many dispersed facts
The model changes its mind overnight
explanation: Synthetic retrieval tests measure a narrow ability. Tasks needing multi-hop reasoning, counting or summarising across the text stress the model differently, so evaluate on tasks that resemble yours.

text: You plan to switch your app to a newer model version. Which rollout is most responsible?
options: Switch all users at once without tests
Run your regression set and shadow or canary traffic, compare quality, cost and latency, then roll out gradually with a rollback path
explanation: Model versions change style, safety behaviour and cost. Offline evaluation, limited exposure and the ability to roll back catch regressions before most users are affected.

text: What is the main idea of a mixture-of-experts (MoE) language model?
options: For each token only a few expert sub-networks are activated, lowering compute per token compared with a dense model of the same total size
It uses one expert for all tokens
explanation: A router selects a few experts per token, so active parameters are fewer than total parameters. Compute per token drops, but memory to hold all experts and routing complexity remain.

text: An assistant calls a search tool before answering. Why is plain 'time to first token' misleading for user experience?
options: The first visible text of the final answer may arrive only after tool latency, so you should trace each stage and the time to first useful text
explanation: In agentic flows the model may think, call tools and then answer. Per-stage tracing (model start, tool time, final answer start) shows where users actually wait.

text: A service saves an order to its database and then publishes an 'order created' event. If it crashes between the two steps, events are lost. Which pattern addresses this?
options: Retry the whole request manually each time
The transactional outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction and publish it from there
explanation: A dual write to two systems cannot be atomic. The outbox stores the event with the data in one transaction, and a relay publishes it at least once, so consumers must handle duplicates (be idempotent).

text: Several microservices read and write the same database tables directly. What is the main problem?
options: They are tightly coupled through the shared schema, so a change in one can break the others and independent deployment is lost
explanation: A common guideline is that each service owns its data and exposes it through an API or events. A shared schema recreates a distributed monolith with the costs of both styles.

text: Your API is being overloaded by a client that retries instantly after errors. Which combination is best practice?
options: Rate-limit with HTTP 429 and a Retry-After header, and have clients back off exponentially with jitter
Increase the timeout to one hour
explanation: Rate limits protect shared capacity, 429 tells clients to slow down, and exponential backoff with random jitter avoids synchronised retry storms.

text: Transaction A locks row 1 then wants row 2; transaction B locks row 2 then wants row 1. PostgreSQL aborts one of them. What is this and how do you reduce it?
options: A deadlock; acquire locks in a consistent order, keep transactions short and retry the aborted one
explanation: Opposite lock orders create a cycle. PostgreSQL detects it and cancels one transaction, so the application must be ready to retry. Consistent ordering and short transactions make deadlocks rarer.

text: A Redis instance restarts and all cached sessions vanish, logging users out. What does this reveal?
options: By default Redis keeps data in memory; you need persistence or replication if the data must survive, or a design where it can be rebuilt
explanation: Redis offers snapshots (RDB) and append-only logs (AOF) plus replication, each with trade-offs in durability and speed. Treat a cache as disposable unless you deliberately configure durability.

text: Conway's law (1967) says that organisations design systems that mirror their own communication structure. What is the practical implication for architecture?
options: Every company needs exactly three teams
Teams should avoid talking to each other
If you want a certain architecture, shape team boundaries and communication to match it
explanation: Four teams building a compiler tend to produce a four-pass compiler. Teams often apply the 'inverse Conway manoeuvre': design team structure to encourage the desired module boundaries.

text: In an 8-bit signed integer using two's complement, what happens when you add 1 to 127?
explanation: The range is −128 to 127. Adding 1 to the largest value overflows into the sign bit and wraps to −128 in languages that wrap silently. Some languages trap or promote to bigger types; know which one you use.

text: What problem did async/await (ES2017) mainly address, building on Promises (ES2015)?
options: It let asynchronous code be written in a readable, sequential style with try/catch error handling
It compiled JavaScript to machine code
explanation: Callbacks led to deeply nested code, Promises flattened chains, and async/await made the flow read top to bottom. It is syntax over Promises; it does not add threads.

text: Which boolean name is least likely to cause bugs and confusion?
explanation: Positive names avoid double negatives like `if (!isNotDisabled)`. Good names say what a value means in the reader's terms; refactoring a negative flag into a positive one often removes a class of mistakes.

text: Why do many people prefer 'open-weights' over 'open-source' for models whose weights are downloadable?
options: Weights alone usually do not include the training data, code and licence freedoms that open source implies
Open source is a trademark of one company
The terms mean exactly the same
explanation: Downloadable weights let you run and often fine-tune a model, but licences may restrict use and the data and training code may be unavailable. 'Open-weights' describes what is actually released.

text: How does SentencePiece differ in spirit from tokenizers that first split text on whitespace?
options: It treats the input as a raw character stream (marking spaces as symbols), so it needs no language-specific word splitting
It stores whole sentences as tokens
explanation: SentencePiece encodes spaces as part of the text, which makes it language-independent and fully reversible. This helps for languages without whitespace-delimited words.

text: Assume an API's rate limit is 200,000 tokens per minute and each request counts its input plus the maximum output you reserve: 3,000 + 500 tokens. About how many requests per minute fit?
explanation: Each request counts 3,500 tokens, and 200,000 ÷ 3,500 ≈ 57. Ignoring the reserved output (200,000 ÷ 3,000 ≈ 66) overestimates. Check how your provider counts limits, and set max output tightly.

text: A chat message contains 20 emoji. How many tokens does it cost?
options: Often more than 20, since many emoji are multi-byte and may span several tokens
explanation: Emoji are multi-byte in UTF-8, and a byte-level tokenizer may split rare ones into several tokens, while common ones can be single tokens. Count with the target tokenizer.

text: What does 'tokenizer fertility' measure for a language?
options: How many babies a language has
The average number of tokens needed per word (or per unit of text), where higher values mean less efficient encoding
The number of letters in the alphabet
explanation: High fertility means more tokens for the same content: higher cost, shorter effective context and sometimes weaker modelling for that language. Comparing fertility across languages exposes tokenizer bias.

text: To benefit from prompt (prefix) caching, how should you order the parts of a prompt?
options: Variable user input first, static instructions last
Static content such as system instructions, tools and reference documents first, and the changing user input last
explanation: Prefix caching reuses an identical beginning, so stable material must come first and anything that changes per request last. A single changed word near the start invalidates the cached prefix.

text: How should a team choose between AI coding tools for its own codebase?
options: Run a trial on real tasks from your repository and measure test pass rates, time saved and review effort
Pick the one with the most advertising
explanation: Public benchmarks may not resemble your code, and some may leak into training data. A small bake-off on your own tasks, with the same acceptance criteria, shows practical value and risks.

text: An assistant can read your email, access private files and send messages. Which combination makes prompt-injection attacks especially dangerous?
options: Only reading public web pages with no tools
Access to private data plus exposure to untrusted content plus the ability to send data outside
explanation: If a malicious email can instruct the assistant to read secrets and send them out, data leaks. Remove one leg: limit tools, require human approval for external actions, or isolate untrusted content.

text: A marketer wants an AI image of a famous actor appearing to endorse a product. What is the main concern?
options: Using a person's likeness without consent and implying an endorsement raises legal and ethical issues
The image will be too colourful
None, AI images are always free of rights
explanation: Likeness, publicity rights and false endorsement rules apply regardless of how an image is made, and platform policies may also prohibit it. Get consent or use original or licensed subjects. This is not legal advice.

text: You must find what changed between two versions of a 60-page contract. Which approach is usually most reliable and economical?
options: Ask the model to compare the full documents from memory
Summarise each version and compare the summaries
Compute a structural diff first, then have the model explain only the changed clauses with their context
explanation: A deterministic diff finds every change exactly and cheaply; the model then interprets the small set of differences. Comparing summaries can miss subtle edits. Legal conclusions still need expert review.

text: An AI search answer about a software package's 'latest version' cites three pages. What should you check?
options: Only the length of the answer
The publication dates of the sources and the package's official release page
explanation: Search results can include stale pages, and the tool may merge old and new information. For fast-changing facts, confirm on the official release page or registry.

text: For standard self-attention, roughly how does compute for the attention step scale when you double the sequence length?
explanation: Self-attention compares every token with every other, so cost grows with the square of sequence length. Efficient attention variants and caching change the constants and sometimes the scaling, but long contexts are still expensive.

text: You cannot change the model. Which app-level technique best reduces misses on facts buried in long inputs?
options: Retrieve and re-rank a small set of passages, and ask the model to extract relevant quotes before answering
explanation: Shrinking and ordering the evidence, then forcing a quote-first step, makes the relevant text explicit before the answer is written. Test the result on your own tasks.

text: A cascade tries a cheap model ($0.20 per 1M tokens) first and escalates to a large one ($3.00 per 1M) when a validator rejects the result, which happens 25% of the time. Assuming equal tokens per call, what is the expected cost per 1M tokens?
explanation: Every request pays the cheap model: $0.20. A quarter also pay the large model: 0.25 × $3.00 = $0.75. Total $0.95, about 32% of always using the large model. The validator's cost and the quality of its judgement must also be counted.

text: Why does serving many concurrent users with very long conversations limit a GPU's throughput?
options: Each active request keeps a large KV cache in memory, so memory limits how many can run at once
explanation: KV-cache memory grows with sequence length for every active request. When memory is full, fewer requests can be batched together, so throughput falls or requests wait.

text: An inference server runs at 95% utilisation and users see TTFT spikes. What explains it, and what is the remedy?
options: TTFT depends only on the user's phone
Queues grow sharply near saturation; keep headroom, add capacity or shed or limit load
explanation: Queueing delays rise steeply as utilisation approaches 100%, even if average capacity looks sufficient. Capacity planning should target headroom for peaks, with autoscaling and admission control.

text: Which Core Web Vitals metric measures how responsive a page is to user interactions throughout the visit?
explanation: INP replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital in 2024 and reflects interaction latency over the page's life. LCP measures loading, CLS measures visual stability and TTFB is server response time.

text: Which is a major cost of sharding a database by user ID?
options: Cross-shard joins and transactions, rebalancing and operational complexity
explanation: Sharding spreads data and load, but anything spanning shards (joins, global uniqueness, transactions) becomes hard, hot keys can overload one shard, and resharding is difficult. Exhaust indexing, caching and replicas before sharding.

text: How should you set HTTP caching for fingerprinted assets like app.3f9a1c.js versus the HTML page that references them?
options: Long caching for the HTML only
Long max-age (even immutable) for the fingerprinted assets, short or revalidated caching for the HTML
The same setting for both, always
explanation: A changed file gets a new name, so old URLs can be cached for a year safely. The HTML must refresh quickly so it points to the newest asset names.

text: Traffic arrives in sharp spikes and overwhelms a slow downstream service. Which design helps most, and what does it cost?
options: Put a queue between them with workers and backpressure; it smooths load but adds latency and requires idempotent processing
explanation: Queues absorb bursts and let workers process at a sustainable rate. In exchange, work completes later, ordering and duplicates need thought, and queue length must be monitored.

text: How would you design a booking flow so that two customers cannot reserve the last seat, even under retries and crashes?
options: Enforce it in the database: an atomic conditional update or a unique constraint on (event, seat), a short-lived hold with expiry, and idempotent confirmation
Use a Redis lock alone and assume it never expires early
Check availability in application code, then insert
Show a warning and hope users agree
explanation: The database is the source of truth, so the rule belongs where it can be enforced atomically. Holds with expiry release abandoned seats, and idempotency keys make retries safe. A lock held only in application memory or cache can be lost or expire mid-operation.
